content: Low back pain (LBP) is an extremely common condition that affects individuals across all age groups, including young people, adults, and older adults. However, the prevalence and associated disability rates are highest among older adults. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides evidence-based recommendations for non-surgical interventions to manage chronic primary LBP in adults, including older individuals. These guidelines also specify interventions that should not be routinely offered as part of standard care. Chronic Primary Low Back Pain: Definition and Significance Chronic primary LBP, previously referred to as non-specific LBP, is defined as pain lasting more than three months that is not attributable to an underlying disease or specific condition. It accounts for over 90% of chronic LBP cases seen in primary care. Up to two-thirds of individuals who experience an acute episode of LBP continue to have symptoms that persist for more than a year, often in a fluctuating pattern. Persistent symptoms are more common in older adults and are associated with reduced physical and mental functioning, negatively impacting quality of life, well-being, and the ability to work or engage socially. Planning and Delivering Care for Chronic Primary LBP 1. Clinical Assessment and Timely Referral: A comprehensive clinical assessment should be conducted from a biopsychosocial perspective by a qualified healthcare professional. This assessment helps identify appropriate interventions and determine when further detailed or urgent clinical review is necessary. 2. Personalized Information and Advice: Patients should receive accurate information about chronic primary LBP and tailored advice to help them understand their pain experience within a biopsychosocial framework. This approach supports re-engagement in meaningful life activities. 3. Tailored Intervention Packages: Effective management often requires a combination of interventions rather than a single isolated approach. The selection and sequencing of interventions should address the physical, psychological, and social factors contributing to the individual’s pain, while also considering their personal context, values, and preferences. Generally, care should begin with the least invasive and least potentially harmful interventions. Non-Surgical Interventions for Chronic Primary LBP The following interventions are relevant for adults, including older individuals, with chronic primary LBP, with or without spine-related leg pain. These interventions are categorized based on their appropriateness for routine care: Interventions That May Be Offered: Education: Structured and standardized education or advice. Physical Interventions: Structured exercise therapies or programs. Needling therapies. Spinal manipulative therapy. Massage. Mobility-assistive products. Psychological Interventions: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Operant therapy. Medicines: Topical capsaicin (Cayenne pepper). Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) antidepressants. Tricyclic antidepressants. White willow (Salix spp.). Other Interventions: Devil’s claw (Harpagophytum procumbens). Interventions That Should Not Be Routinely Used: Traction. Therapeutic ultrasound. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS). Lumbar braces, belts, or supports. Injectable local anesthetics. Glucocorticoids. Skeletal muscle relaxants. Anticonvulsants. Opioid analgesics. Summary The WHO guidelines emphasize a holistic, patient-centered approach to managing chronic primary LBP in primary and community care settings. Care should be tailored to the individual’s needs, starting with the least invasive options and addressing the multifactorial nature of LBP.
